claim: Across 117,062 dependency changes from agent-authored and human-authored PRs on 2,807 GitHub repos across seven ecosystems, AI coding agents select known-vulnerable dependency versions more often than humans: 2.46% vs 1.64% of additions/updates.
stance_target: assumption that autonomous coding agents maintain dependency security at least as well as human developers
scope_conditions: 117,062 dependency changes, 33,596 agent PRs (Copilot, Devin, OpenAI Codex, Cursor, Claude Code) vs 6,618 human PRs, 2,807 repos, 7 ecosystems, AIDev-pop dataset
quoted_support: Agents select known-vulnerable versions more often than humans (2.46% vs. 1.64%)

claim: When AI agents introduce a vulnerable dependency version, remediation is harder than for humans: 36.8% of agent cases require a major-version upgrade to reach a patched release, versus 12.9% for human cases.
stance_target: blast radius of agent-driven code changes being systematically larger/harder to remediate than human changes
scope_conditions: same dataset, PR-time vulnerability labeling via ecosyste.ms (GitHub Security Advisories + OSV)
quoted_support: their vulnerable selections are more disruptive to remediate (36.8% require major-version upgrades vs. 12.9% for humans), despite patched alternatives existing in most cases.

claim: At the fleet level, agent-authored dependency work produced a net vulnerability increase of 98 across the sample, while human-authored dependency work produced a net vulnerability reduction of 1,316 over the same period.
stance_target: assumption that autonomous agents improve overall supply-chain security posture through routine dependency maintenance
scope_conditions: aggregate across 2,807 repos, same study period
quoted_support: At the aggregate level, agent-driven dependency work yields a net vulnerability increase of 98, whereas human-authored work yields a net reduction of 1,316.

claim: AI agents perform dependency version updates more frequently than humans when touching a manifest file (25.5% vs 15.8%), but spread edits across many small PRs rather than bundling them as humans do.
stance_target: characterizing agent PR behavior patterns relevant to CI/CD trigger design
quoted_support: agents spread dependency edits across many PRs and, within those edits, perform version updates more often than humans (25.5% vs. 15.8%).

claim: The study authors recommend PR-time vulnerability screening and registry-aware guardrails as the mitigation for agent-introduced dependency risk, directly motivating an automated blast-radius/adversarial-review gate before merge in autonomous development pipelines.
stance_target: necessity of rigid, automated pre-merge security gates in an AI software factory architecture
scope_conditions: recommendation derived from the empirical findings above
quoted_support: These findings motivate PR-time vulnerability screening and registry-aware guardrails to make agent-driven dependency updates safer.
